title: The beloved son (Luke 20:1–19)
hookLine: the tenants kill the owner's son; the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone

cards: The last week. Jesus is teaching in the temple courts every day, and the leaders come with a sharp question: by what authority do you do these things?
He answers with a question about John the Baptist that they can't answer without trouble either way. So nobody answers. Then he tells the crowd a story.
A man plants a vineyard, rents it to tenant farmers, and goes away a long time. At harvest he sends a servant for his share. The tenants beat him and send him back empty.
A second, the same. A third, wounded and thrown out.

teach.h: THREE SERVANTS, THEN THE BELOVED SON.
teach.b: In the King James Bible, the owner thinks out loud: "What shall I do? I will send my beloved son: it may be they will reverence him when they see him." Three servants beaten, and he sends the person he loves most.
Not a clever plan. A hopeful one, maybe a foolish one.

teach.h: THE TENANTS: THIS IS THE HEIR.
teach.b: The tenants reason the other way: this is the heir, kill him, and the vineyard is ours. They throw him out and kill him.

Some in that crowd may have known the picture: in Isaiah, Israel is God's vineyard, planted with care. And beloved has been heard before in Luke: at the river, a voice from heaven called Jesus "my beloved Son."

teach.h: A STORY AIMED AT A FEW LEADERS.
teach.b: So Christians hear the story pointing at the one telling it.
Luke says plainly who heard it as aimed at them: the chief priests and the scribes, who wanted to arrest him that hour and held back because they feared the people. Not a whole nation.
A small circle of leaders in one tense week. Christians have sometimes forgotten that and turned this parable against Jewish people, and some churches have since said so with regret.

teach.h: THE REJECTED STONE HOLDS IT ALL.
teach.b: Then Jesus quotes a psalm: "The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner."

teach.h: THE STONE WHICH THE BUILDERS REJECTED.
teach.b: The builders toss a stone aside as useless; later it holds the whole building together. The rejection isn't the end of the story. It's the turn.

how: Churches that follow a lectionary read the parable of the wicked tenants in their cycle of readings, and Psalm 118, with its rejected stone, is traditionally sung at Easter.

games.q: what's inside Luke 20:1–19 — tap the pairs.
p: beat the servants, killed the son
became the head of the corner

s: Luke says the parable was aimed at the whole Jewish people
Luke says the chief priests and the scribes perceived it was spoken against them, and that they feared the people.
the owner sends three servants before his son
each is beaten and sent back empty. then he sends the one he loves.
the cornerstone line is Jesus quoting a psalm
it comes from Psalm 118, a psalm of thanksgiving.

games.q: you own the vineyard. three servants have come home beaten and empty-handed. what do you do?
o: send soldiers to throw the tenants out.
send your beloved son, hoping they'll respect him.
games.why: "I will send my beloved son: it may be they will reverence him when they see him." a hopeful choice, and the tenants kill him.

practice: Think of something you set aside as useless: a person you wrote off at work, an idea you dropped because someone laughed, a part of yourself you keep hidden.
Turn it over in your mind like a builder with a stone, more slowly than the first time, and wonder whether this is the one that holds things together. If you pray, bring it to God and leave it there.

wordCard.voice: Isaiah, the prophet whose picture of Israel as God's vineyard lies behind the parable of the owner's beloved son.

orig.note: Greek: beloved, dearly loved. the same word the voice from heaven uses at Jesus's baptism in Luke 3:22.

carryVoice: Your line: they will respect my son. Love kept on sending. Day five hundred seventy-two.
